question: What is the primary goal of triage in an emergency department?

options.A: Sorting patients based on injury severity

explanation: Triage prioritizes care so that patients with the most life-threatening conditions receive immediate medical attention. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h1)

question: Why must a triage nurse keep monitoring patients who are waiting in the emergency queue?

options.A: Doctors refuse to see patients without updated charts
options.B: Waiting patients often complain about the slow service
options.C: A stable patient's condition can suddenly get worse
options.D: Hospital policy requires a vital sign check every five minutes

explanation: Illness can change quickly! Someone who looks stable at first triage can crash suddenly and need immediate help. Keep a close eye on your patients. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h1)

question: What does the letter 'C' stand for in the ABCDE primary survey?
explanation: In the ABCDE framework, C stands for circulation, which involves checking pulses, bleeding, and perfusion. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h2)

question: A patient arrives at the emergency unit with severe trauma. Following the ABCDE approach, what should you check first?
explanation: Always follow the alphabet! Airway comes first before anything else because getting oxygen flowing is our top priority. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h2)

question: Why is opening the airway the top priority in emergency care?

options.A: It prevents patients from talking too loudly
options.B: Blocked air passages quickly lead to brain death
options.C: It stops internal bone bleeding immediately
options.D: Doctors cannot write prescriptions without it

explanation: Without a clear airway, oxygen cannot reach the brain. Brain cells start dying in minutes without oxygen, so we must clear the airway first! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h3)

question: When would a nurse use an oropharyngeal airway device?

options.A: In an unconscious patient lacking gag reflexes
options.B: To suction mucus from a patient's stomach
options.C: To deliver oral medications for high blood pressure
options.D: In a conscious patient who is talking normally

explanation: These airways can make an awake patient vomit. We only use them on deeply unconscious patients who won't gag on it. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h3)

question: What is the main problem happening in all types of shock?

options.A: Inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery
options.B: Elevated blood sugar levels in the bloodstream
options.C: Sudden swelling of the upper respiratory tract
options.D: High fever caused by a bacterial infection

explanation: Simply put, shock means the body's tissues aren't getting enough blood and oxygen to survive and do their work. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h4)

question: Why might a patient in early shock still have a normal blood pressure reading?

options.A: Blood pressure monitors are usually inaccurate in emergencies
options.B: Kidneys immediately stop producing urine to save pressure
options.C: Fluid volume only affects the health of the heart
options.D: The body uses compensatory mechanisms like vasoconstriction

explanation: Our amazing bodies fight back! The nervous system tightens blood vessels and speeds up the heart to keep blood pressure normal at first, even if fluid is low. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h4)

question: When should a nurse perform the secondary survey on an emergency patient?

options.A: While the patient is still arriving through the ambulance door
options.B: After life threats are treated and the patient is stable
options.C: Only after the doctor has discharged the patient home
options.D: Before checking if the patient has a clear airway

explanation: ABCDE comes first! We only do a detailed head-to-toe secondary survey once immediate life threats are under control. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h5)

question: What information does the 'L' stand for in the SAMPLE history checklist?

options.A: Last oral intake of food or fluids
options.C: Level of pain reported by the patient
options.D: Length of time the symptoms lasted

explanation: In SAMPLE, L means 'Last meal or drink'. This is super important just in case the patient needs emergency surgery with anesthesia! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h5)

question: Which drug route is usually used when you cannot find an emergency IV line?
explanation: When an IV is impossible, we can drill right into the bone marrow (IO) to deliver emergency drugs super fast into circulation. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h6)

question: Why do nurses prefer IV medications over oral tablets during severe emergencies?

options.A: It is completely painless for the patient
options.B: It delivers medication directly into the bloodstream for fast action
options.C: Oral medications are illegal in hospital emergency units
options.D: It eliminates the need for any dosage calculations

explanation: IV meds skip the digestive system completely, hitting the bloodstream instantly when every single second counts. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h6)

question: What legal idea allows you to treat an unconscious trauma patient without their verbal permission?
explanation: The law assumes that if an unconscious person could speak, they would definitely want you to save their life! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h7)

question: Why is writing clear, real-time notes so important in emergency nursing?

options.A: It provides a clear legal record of all care provided
options.B: Doctors use the nurse's notes to diagnose diseases
options.C: It replaces the need for verbal shift handovers
options.D: It guarantees that the hospital insurance claim gets paid

explanation: Good documentation protects your patient's ongoing care and acts as legal proof in court of the great nursing care you delivered. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T7#GNS112_U7_T7_h7)
